newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: FEATURE-Grandmother senator winning Argentine hearts.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Grandmother senator winning Argentine hearts.

text.p: In a country bewitched by teenaged fashion models and plastic surgery, a 66-year-old teacher untroubled by the big bags under her eyes is turning heads.

"Someone has to grow old in this country," said Graciela Fernandez Meijide, a centre-left senator who has become Argentina's most popular politician and who is challenging the Peronists in Buenos Aires province, their main stronghold.

The Peronist fiefdom surrounding the capital is home to 40 percent of Argentines and the place where national elections are won or lost. There, the compassionate and straight-talking style of a woman whose face shows the pain of losing a son to the military in their "Dirty War" of the 1970s is winning over an electorate tired of male politicians who are frivolous or tainted by corruption allegations.

Fernandez Meijide announced in early March she would leave her seat as a Buenos Aires city senator to run for the Chamber of Deputies representing her Frepaso coalition in Buenos Aires province in October's mid-term congressional elections.

Already the polls show she is leading the ruling Peronists by five percentage points and one survey gave her an approval rating among the residents of the capital and province of 63 percent, compared to just 19 percent for Peronist President Carlos Menem.

"The inconceivable -- the Peronists losing in what was supposed to be their fortress in Buenos Aires province -- is now a possibility that nobody can afford the luxury of denying," political analyst James Neilson said. "That reality alone has transformed Argentina's political map."
OPPOSITION IN DISARRAY

Fernandez Meijide's candidacy has sent the Peronists and the Radical Party, the country's second largest political force, scrambling for a fresh face to spare them a humiliating defeat in October. But their worries go even further: the name of Graciela, as she is known to the public, is already being touted for the 1999 presidential election, in which Menem cannot run again.

If she ran, she would be the first woman ever to run for Argentina's presidency. The only woman president was Maria Estela Martinez de Peron, known as Isabelita, who succeeded her husband Gen. Juan Peron on his death in 1974. Her term was characterised by political violence and was cut short by a military coup in 1976.

Local analysts scratch their heads over how Fernandez Meijide has gone from obscure centre-left hopeful in legislative elections five years ago to possible presidential candidate. Even she acknowledges that it is all "dizzying." But she makes no bones about her ambition: "I didn't enter politics not to fight for power."
Leading political commentator Mariano Grondona says the senator "embodies what Argentina still sorely lacks: ethics and a challenge to corruption."
Menem's 8-year-old administration has won praise worldwide for promoting economic reforms and stability but is regularly under fire for high-level corruption scandals.
SON KIDNAPPED AND PROBABLY MURDERED

Fernandez Meijide's rise may have been meteoric but she began the long slog of political activism nearly two decades ago when her 17-year-old son Pablo was kidnapped and presumably killed by the military during their terror campaign against leftists.

She became a member of the Permanent Assembly for Human Rights and the National Comission on the Disappearance of People, which in the 1980s investigated crimes perpetrated by the military, leading to their trial and brief imprisonment.

But she joined a political party only in 1990, signing up with the centre-left Frente Grande, now the Frepaso. In 1993 she entered the lower house of Congress after the Frepaso won 13.6 percent of the vote in legislative elections and in 1995 she won a Senate seat for the city of Buenos Aires with 45.6 percent of the vote, the most a woman ever got in an election in Argentina.

Eduardo Van der Kooy, political columnist for the Clarin newspaper, said her strongest attributes are her "austere style, straight talk and common sense." Sociologist and pollster Manuel Mora y Araujo points to her "moderation, sensitivity, austerity and honesty."

But many wonder how this language teacher, married to the poet and architect Enrique Fernandez Meijides for nearly five decades, would fare in presidential elections without a nationwide party structure and lacking a firm grasp on issues such as economics or international politics.

"On the economic front she shares the ambiguity of the Frepaso," Jorge Blanco Villegas of the powerful UIA business lobby said. "Some of her comments seem to support the (orthodox) economic model while others point to a fierce opposition."

Rather than fighting those allegations, Fernandez Meijide acknowledges her shortcomings. "In politics it is difficult to find a man who can admit he ignores a few things," she said. "Not knowing, in a woman, is not seen as quite as bad."
